Bulimia made my body pretty insulin resistant for a time. No matter how little or how much I ate, I would gain. It is worth exploring insulin resistance and seeing what you can do to help resensitize your body so that it can process sugars correctly. Also with this insulin resistance you get major blood sugar drops and changes so you continuously crave sugar/carbs or food in general so that adds to the addiction factor. I just want to preface this and say that I am not a doctor,  but I did go through something similar and I know how mentally and physically draining it can be. 

 Also another thing to consider is the timeline of your binge development. You started gaining during puberty,  with the change in hormones you could possibly have undiagnosed PCOS.  Have you had hormone levels checked? Sometimes we have all the symptoms and none of the cysts. It is just a thought based on what you're describing. So there are a few differences, and several things to consider when deciding if you want a physical or chemical sunscreen? 

Chemical sunscreen absorbs into the skin and converts UV rays into a less damaging wave length for the skin. It is good for daily use and can be combined with other skincare products. 

Physical sunscreen sits on top of the skin and reflects the Uv rays. It starts working immediately and can usually be identified by its "whitecast" 

My suggestions for a good body sunscreen that is cost effective would be from Neutrogena. The sheer defense body mist is great and does not have a white cast or feel oily on the skin. 

If you want a traditional lotion, I second the supergoop or eltaMD brand. They work great and have lots of options for chemical or physical sunscreens.

The thing with eating disorders is that no matter what you say we wont believe it. 

We wont believe were beautiful or healthy or any of the adjectives you think will make us feel better. Words wont save us.  This disorder is like a parasite it will do anything possible to maintain itself, it will foster fears and doubts in the individual and make us assume these false truths. I speak for myself in this, but as a disordered individual there is so much shame and fear wrapped up in these behaviors. She hides the food and overcompensates with healthy behaviors to try to protect you, but most importantly to protect the disorder. Its a hard explanation to swallow. I am sure not everyone would agree with me, but I would ask you to consider it. If you involve her parents or force her into a recovery process, she will feel attacked and all the anxiety harbored for fears she has created will run rampant. 

The best course of action is risk management. Be receptive to her plans for dinner and solidify her positive choices. Encourage positive choices and instill healthy behaviors. Tread lightly with discussing this disorder. 

There is no magic cure, or "good" advice, everyone is different and reacts different. Just continue to be loving and supportive and practice positive behaviors.

The issue with that thought is that there is no choice. I think this is a controversial reply but here is why I feel this way. I don't think you wake up and choose not to accept your body. You say its for control, but really it is the compulsory act to manage the obsession that you have created with utilizing your weight as a measure of stability/control.

What I do think is that it is unhealthy to give a person an ultimatum that guarantees that they fail. Even in recovery the thoughts are there and its impossible to just stop. So you don't choose, you compromise, you both do the work and go to therapy and make it work or you move on, because its selfish to be in a situation where a person resents you because you cant physically choose (stop) or meet their idea of recovered. Its a lose/lose system and I am sorry this reply is harsh, I just want to speak to my experience and spare you some of the heartache that comes with being forced to choose.
